title: Matter and Particles
seo_title: Grade 3 Science: Matter and Particles Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: All matter is made of particles: matter has mass and takes up space, atoms are the building blocks of matter, and the particles in solids, liquids and gases are arranged differently. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 3, Chemistry)
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 science worksheets (BC): what matter is, solids, liquids and gases, particles in matter and changes of state. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: All matter is made of tiny particles.
key_sub: Matter has mass and takes up space.
body_html:
How to think about it

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space: a rock, water and air are all matter. Everything is made of tiny particles, too small to see. Atoms are the building blocks.

In a solid the particles are packed tightly and vibrate in place, so it keeps its shape. In a liquid they slide past each other, so it flows. In a gas they are far apart and move fast, so it fills its container.

Example

Is air matter?

Does it take up space? Blow up a balloon.

Answer: yes

Example

In which state are the particles farthest apart?

Think of steam.

Answer: gas

Common mistakes

  • Thinking air is nothing.
  • Thinking particles in a solid do not move at all (they vibrate).
  • Thinking light and heat are matter.

faq.q: Why can a gas be squeezed?
faq.a: Its particles are far apart, so they can be pushed closer together.

faq.q: Why does a liquid take the shape of its cup?
faq.a: Its particles can slide past each other.

items.q: Which property describes how easily a material bends without breaking?
items.e: Rubber is flexible.

items.q: What is matter?
c: anything that has mass and takes up space
items.e: Air is matter too.

items.q: Is a block of wood a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Which of these is a gas?
items.e: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Snow disappears on a sunny winter day without melting. What happened?
c: It sublimated, turning straight into water vapour.
items.e: Sublimation skips the liquid state.

items.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
items.e: Gas particles move freely.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps the same volume but changes shape?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which state of matter can be squashed into a smaller space?

items.q: Which state of matter has a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
items.e: Solids keep their shape.

items.q: Which state of matter flows and takes the shape of its container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Is a glass marble a solid, a liquid or a gas?

items.q: Which of these is a liquid?

items.q: When ice melts, what happens to its mass?
items.e: Changes of state do not change mass.

items.q: A 40 g glass marble is heated and expands. What happens to its density?
c: It decreases, because the same mass takes up a larger volume.
It stays the same, because the mass is the same.
It increases, because the particles get bigger.
It increases, because the mass increases.
items.e: Density = mass ÷ volume. The volume increases while the mass stays the same.

items.q: A dented ping-pong ball pops back into shape in hot water. Which explains this?
c: The particles themselves become bigger when heated.
The air particles inside move faster and further apart, pushing the dent out.
The mass of the substance increases when heated.
items.e: Particles move faster and further apart when heated; they do not grow and no new particles form.

items.q: Which state of matter cannot be poured and keeps its shape?
items.e: Use the particle model: arrangement, movement and forces.

items.q: A tea bag is put into hot water and the colour spreads. What is the best explanation?
c: The particles were pushed by convection only.
Diffusion: tea particles diffused into the water.
The particles grew bigger and filled the space.
The water or air particles stopped moving.
items.e: Particles are always moving randomly, so there is a net movement from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.

items.q: A 40 g copper block is heated and expands. What happens to the size of its particles?
items.e: Only the spaces between the particles increase.

items.q: Power cables sag more on a hot afternoon. Which explains this?
c: The mass of the substance increases when heated.
The particles themselves become bigger when heated.
The cables expand and become longer when heated.
items.e: Particles move faster and further apart when heated; they do not grow and no new particles form.
